text.text: Run the shop from here. Every repair order is tied to a vehicle, so the whole history of a car (mileage, past work, what the customer declined) is one click away. The service advisor writes the order, gets approval, and Mark done closes it at pickup. Fleet accounts pay on terms; sent and overdue invoices both count in Awaiting payment.

pages.title: Start here: how this workspace runs

text.text: A ten-minute tour of how the shop's work flows through this workspace. Share it with the service advisors, the shop manager and every technician.
What lives where
Customers
: drivers and fleet accounts, with what they owe and how many repair orders are open.
Vehicles
: each car, truck and van, with VIN, plate, mileage and the next oil change. Every repair order for that vehicle is listed on its card.
Repair orders
: the complaint, the vehicle, the technician, the estimate, approval, declined work, parts and labor cost, and margin.
Parts stock
: oil, filters, brakes, batteries and the rest of the shelf, with reorder points.
Invoices
: what each repair order billed, paid and owed. Fleet invoices carry terms.
A repair order from counter to pickup
The advisor writes the order as
New request
, with the vehicle and mileage in.
The technician diagnoses; the advisor builds the estimate and gets approval (
Customer approved
). A technician can press
Assign to me
Parts arrive, work is done. Waiting on parts means
On hold
Quality check and road test, then
Mark done
at pickup.
Payment at the counter, or an invoice on terms for fleets. Past due becomes
Overdue
; Awaiting payment counts sent and overdue.
Mark paid
stamps the date.
Your rhythm
Every morning: Dashboard, today's appointments, orders waiting for approval
Every afternoon: call every drop-off customer with a status before 3 pm
Every Friday: shelf count, cores and returns
Every month: comebacks, thin margins, and declined work to follow up
Making it yours

Rename work types to the jobs you do most, add your parts suppliers, and delete the sample customers once a dozen of your own are in. Type in any cell or drag cards between columns; every total updates by itself.
An invoice can be higher than the first estimate when the customer approves extra work at the counter; keep the estimate as written so the margin compares what you sold with what it cost.
Bays this week, revenue by type of work and open invoices.

pages.title: Writing a repair order and estimate

text.text: The repair order is a contract. Write the customer's words, test before you sell, and never touch a wrench without approval.
At the counter
Find the customer and pick the
Vehicle
(or add it: year, make and model, VIN, plate). Write
Mileage in
from the dash, not from memory.
Write the complaint in the customer's own words: "grinding from the back when I stop," not "needs brakes."
Ask when it happens: cold or warm, at what speed, turning or straight, for how long.
Set
Waiting or drop-off
. Waiters get a time promise; drop-offs get a call by a set hour.
Check the vehicle's earlier repair orders. Declined work from last time is the first thing to mention.
Diagnose before you estimate
Charge for diagnosis. A check-engine light is not a part number. Say up front what the diagnostic costs and that it comes off the repair if they go ahead.
The technician writes the cause and the test that proved it on the order: the code, the freeze-frame, the reading.
Photos of worn parts next to a new one sell more honestly than any script.
Building the estimate
Parts at your price, with your markup.
Labor from a published labor guide, times your door rate.
Shop supplies and disposal, and tax.
Split it into
must do now
(safety, the complaint),
should do soon
, and
can wait
Enter the estimate, parts cost, labor cost and hours. Under 20 percent margin shows as Thin; on parts-heavy jobs check your markup first.
Getting approval
Call or text the estimate with photos. When the customer says yes, tick
Customer approved
and write who approved it and when. Anything they put off goes in
Declined work
; it is the first thing the advisor brings up next visit.
Example

A 2012 wagon comes in with a flashing check-engine light. The diagnostic finds a misfire on cylinder 3; swapping coils moves the misfire, so the coil is bad. The advisor texts a photo and the estimate: coil and plugs now, the valve cover gasket seep can wait. The customer approves the coil and plugs. Next time the car is in, the advisor opens the order and sees the gasket on the declined list.
Never do this
Add work without approval, even small items.
Promise a time you have not checked with the technician.
Write "check and advise" with no complaint behind it.
Parts are where shops quietly lose money: wrong parts, slow returns, and cores left in the back. A simple routine fixes all three.
What to keep on the shelf
Oil in your top three weights, the filters for the vehicles you see most, cabin and engine air filters
Brake pads and rotors for your most common vehicles, brake fluid, brake clean
Batteries in the two or three groups that fit most cars in your area
Wiper blades, bulbs, belts, coolant, and common fuses
Everything else comes from the parts store, usually within an hour.
Ordering for a repair order
Order with the VIN, not just year, make and model. Many models change parts mid-year.
Put the parts cost on the repair order as soon as it is known, so the margin is right.
If a part is more than a day out, set the order
On hold
and tell the customer the date.
Check the part against the old one before installing. Wrong parts are returned the same day.
Cores and returns
Every core (batteries, alternators, starters, calipers) tagged with the repair order number
Returns and cores go back on the next delivery run, never later than the end of the week
Return credits checked against the store statement every month
The weekly count
On Friday the shop manager counts the shelf and types the real count into
On hand
. Anything showing
Reorder
goes on Monday's stock order. Look at the Stock value column once a quarter: slow parts on the shelf are cash you cannot spend.
Warranty on parts
Keep failed parts that are under warranty, tagged with the vehicle, mileage and date. Parts stores will not credit a warranty claim without the old part.
Example

On Thursday a delivery fleet's van needs front pads and rotors. The rotors on the shelf do not match the VIN's brake package, so the advisor orders the right ones by VIN for a 2 pm delivery. The wrong pair stays on the shelf for the next van of that model. The old rotors go in the scrap bin, and the caliper core goes back with Friday's run.
Pickup is where the customer decides whether they trust you. A clean car, a clear invoice and five minutes of explanation bring them back.
Before you call the customer
Road test the vehicle and confirm the complaint is fixed
Torque the wheels to spec on any job that had them off
Check for leaks under the car after the test drive
Reset the oil life and any warning lights you were asked to clear
Remove seat covers, floor paper and the steering wheel cover
Old parts in a box in the trunk if the customer asked for them
Update
Mileage at last visit
and
Next oil change at
on the vehicle
Explaining the invoice

Walk the customer through the work in plain words: what was wrong, what you did, and what you saw that they should plan for. Point at the declined work you wrote down. Never pressure: "this can wait until spring" builds more trust than a scare.
Closing the order
Press
Mark done
: it stamps the completion date.
Take payment and press
Mark paid
on the invoice. Fleet accounts get the invoice set to
Sent
with their terms; past their due date it becomes
Overdue
, and their Awaiting payment shows both.
Book the next visit if one is due.
Comebacks
A car that returns within 90 days for the same problem is a comeback. Open a new repair order, tick
Comeback

, and give it to the technician who did the work, with the shop manager looking over it. Comebacks show on the Dashboard; review them every month. Most come from a missed second cause (two bad coils, not one), a part from a weak brand, or a test that was skipped.
Example

A customer picks up her pickup after a new battery. The advisor shows her the test printout from the old battery, mentions that the serpentine belt is cracked and can wait a month, and books her in for it. Two weeks later she calls to move the appointment up, because she trusts the shop's timing.
Thank-you and follow-up
The day after pickup, send a short text: "Thanks for coming in. Anything we should know about the car?" It catches problems while they are small and earns the review.
